newsitem.title: ANGOLA: UNITA again offers semi-compliance with peace deal.
newsitem.headline: UNITA again offers semi-compliance with peace deal.

text.p: Angola's rebel UNITA leader Jonas Savimbi failed on Tuesday to keep a promise to U.N. peacebrokers that he would send all UNITA members of parliament to the Angolan capital to form a national unity government.
Formation of the government -- the key final step in the 1994 peace pact to end the war between UNITA and the Angolan government -- has been delayed three times since January, mainly by Savimbi.

Savimbi promised on Monday that "all of our remaining deputies" would show up in Luanda, leading the country to expect that 21 UNITA representatives still missing from the rebel movement's full contingent of 70 officials would arrive.
However, UNITA radio said nine deputies and four UNITA had made the trip, and the rest would travel as soon as "administrative procedures" had been sorted out.

Clouding the reasons for this latest delay, an aide to Savimbi in Luanda explained that some of those who did not arrive on Tuesday were in fear of their lives in the capital, stronghold of the MPLA government of President Jose Eduardo dos Santos.
"Dr Savimbi cannot force these people to come if they don't want to. They fear for their lives. They are truly scared to come here," UNITA's Abel Chivukuvuku told Reuters.

Diplomats said that was a scarcely credible excuse. They pointed to the fact that UNITA officials have been in Luanda since soon after the signing of the peace pact in 1994, and that over 50 representatives from UNITA were now on hand in Luanda to take part in the joint parliament.

The U.N. Security Council has threatened sanctions against UNITA unless it stops dragging its feet in implementing a peace plan. Savimbi made his latest promise to visiting U.N. Secretary General Kofi Annan, who reminded the UNITA leader of the pledge in a speech he made on Tuesday to the Angolan National Assembly.
"I hope that by tomorrow evening, as was promised to me by Dr Savimbi yesterday in Bailundo, all remaining members of UNITA who are not with us today will be here," Annan told parliament.
UNITA (the National Union for the Total Independence of Angola) and the MPLA government signed a peace treaty in Zambia in 1994 to end nearly two decades of civil war.
But Savimbi himself has refused to travel to Luanda because, he says, he fears for his life. On Monday, he repeated that the unity government will be sworn in without him.

Chivukuvuku said UNITA had proposed to the government that the new unity administration be sworn in on March 29. The date of the ceremony has been put back three times from the original January 25 proposal.
"We proposed that we do it on the 29th, now it is up to the government...they must decide what date they want," he told Reuters.
Diplomats attending Tuesday's joint parliamentary sitting said Savimbi had obviously not kept his word to the U.N. chief.
"It doesn't build confidence to make promises and not keep them. But, look around you, there are more than 50 UNITA deputies here, that is something, that is progress," one Western diplomat said.
